original_content: Notes from reading the Vectorize internals blog. The metadata index uses a sparse inverted index over the metadata column, separate from the dense vector store. Filter cardinality of <1% slows query latency 2-3x because it forces post-filter rather than pre-filter. Implication: scope filter on Engram (binary personal/project/org) is fine; finer-grained filters (type, source) should stay metadata-search-only. Index limits: max 4 metadata indexes; declare all at index-creation time. Cosine metric is the default for bge-base-en-v1.5; do not override. ~2400 chars of distilled notes follow on indexing internals, the LSM-tree-backed storage layer, query planning rules, the relationship between metadata cardinality and ms-per-query, the role of pre-filtering vs post-filtering, the difference between sparse and dense indexes, and the impact of the cosine metric on edge cases like zero-norm vectors. Quotes from the blog: "queries with low-cardinality filters can be 2-3x slower"; "index limits are intentional — they shape the query plan"; "prefer binary metadata for high-throughput". My takeaway: keep Engram's scope metadata as binary buckets; do NOT add a memory_type metadata index until v0.2 when we have enough memories per type to make it worthwhile.
paraphrased_query: what did I learn about Vectorize metadata filter cardinality

expected_extracted_fields.title: Vectorize internals — metadata filter cardinality
expected_extracted_fields.summary: Low-cardinality metadata filters force post-filter (2-3x slower); keep scope as binary buckets; max 4 metadata indexes; bge-base-en-v1.5 default cosine
